Failure rate functions M(T)

Source: R/discrete-time-hazard-brms.R
M_catalogue.Rd

This catalogue contains every function the failure rate may take: the nine failure rate functions M(T) of Kingsolver and Umbanhowar (2018, Table 1), each catalogue key named for its model there. Without a threshold: const (a constant rate), exp (exponential), zeroexp (exponential minus its value at the reference temperature Tr, so the rate is zero there), power (a power of temperature above a baseline rate) and zeropower (the same power with no baseline, zero at Tr). The threshold variants const_threshold, exp_threshold, zeroexp_threshold and zeropower_threshold hold the rate at zero below a fitted critical temperature Tc; above Tc it is constant for const_threshold and accelerates for the other three. The exponential functions give a straight thermal death time curve, whereas the power functions give a curved one.

Usage

M_catalogue

Format

A named list, one entry per failure rate function M(T).

Details

Tr (T0 in Kingsolver and Umbanhowar's notation) is a single reference temperature set for the whole model, not the per-trial starting temperature. The exponential is anchored at Tr and the zero forms vanish there, but because the failure rate must depend only on the current temperature, Tr cannot be each trial's own starting temperature. Trials that begin at different temperatures (acclimation groups, field conditions) enter through their temperature trajectories, not through Tr.

To keep fitting, simulation and reporting from diverging, all three evaluate the same expression strings, which are held in brms_log_M.

Each entry gives the integer the Stan code dispatches on (stan_id), the parameters the function needs (dpars), and the steepness of the threshold switch (k_sw). The rate parameters a, b and c are represented on the log scale (loga, logb, logc), so the linear predictor is unconstrained and their strictly positive values are recovered by exponentiation; the critical temperature Tc is left on the natural scale, since it is not sign-constrained. k_sw is roughly the inverse of the width of the transition in temperature, so a larger value is a sharper switch over a narrower band. The switch is smoothed rather than hard because Stan fits the model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, which explores the posterior by following the gradient of the log-density with respect to each parameter; the gradient of a hard step with respect to the critical temperature is zero on either side of it and undefined at the step itself, so the sampler gets no slope to move that temperature along, whereas a smooth switch supplies one.

The units of M(T)

The hazard is h0(tau) M(T), and which of the two factors carries the unit of reciprocal time depends on the baseline (see h0_catalogue). With the memoryless and Gompertz baselines h0(tau) has no unit, so M(T) is a rate per unit time, and a is the failure rate at the temperature where M(T) = a. With the Weibull and log-logistic baselines h0(tau) is itself per unit time, so M(T) is a multiplier with no unit; with the Weibull, a is the cumulative hazard reached over the reference time at that temperature. The value of a therefore cannot be compared between models with different baselines, nor between datasets timed in different units when the baseline is memoryless or Gompertz.

Whatever the baseline, survival at a constant temperature is exp(-M(T) H0(tau)), with H0 the cumulative baseline hazard. derive_tdt_ttl() derives the critical thermal maximum, the thermal death time curves and the thermal tolerance landscape from that expression, and those can be compared between models.

References

Kingsolver, J. G. and Umbanhowar, J. (2018). The analysis and interpretation of critical temperatures. Journal of Experimental Biology 221, jeb167858. doi:10.1242/jeb.167858
